title: Cascading failure from overload after a heat wave — July 2026
summary: A grid overload driven by cooling demand triggered a cascading failure that hit several dependent elements in under 10 minutes.
outcome: The repair took 45 minutes because the origin substation was not identified until 15 minutes in. Lesson: when several elements fail almost simultaneously, first check whether they share the same origin substation before treating them as independent incidents.

title: Partial restoration that created a false sense of resolution — March 2026
summary: Grid voltage partially recovered (60%) after a first repair, which led the system to lower the incident's priority before the repair was complete.
outcome: The grid went down again 20 minutes later, creating a second crisis peak. Lesson: do not close or deprioritize a substation incident until grid voltage stays stable above 90% for at least 5 minutes.

title: Crew diverted mid-route by a new priority — May 2026
summary: A crew already en route to the substation was redirected to a hospital by a sudden emergency, delaying the substation repair.
outcome: The substation repair was delayed 22 minutes, prolonging the crisis for every element depending on it. Lesson: diverting a crew heading to the root cause (substation) is only justified if the new destination is more critical than fixing the blackout's origin for everyone else.

title: Crew could not reach the substation switchyard — February 2026
summary: A crew assigned to restore a substation was stopped at the perimeter because the switchyard gate was locked and no key holder was on the dispatch list. The grid_voltage stayed low while the crew waited outside.
outcome: A key holder was reached after 17 minutes and the repair began. Lesson: confirm access and a key holder before dispatching a crew to a substation; a locked switchyard delays every dependent of that grid_voltage.

title: Repair crew sent to the wrong substation in the ring — April 2026
summary: The dispatch confused two substations with similar names and the crew began work at a healthy site while the failed one kept its grid_voltage near zero.
outcome: The error was noticed 13 minutes in and the crew rerouted. Lesson: confirm the substation id and its current grid_voltage before assigning a crew; a crew at the wrong ring does not restore anyone.

title: Cascading failure treated as independent incidents — June 2026
summary: A substation failure dropped grid_voltage at several dependents, and each dependent was escalated as a separate incident before the shared origin was identified.
outcome: Resources were scattered across the dependents for 18 minutes before the crew was sent to the origin. Lesson: when several sites lose grid_voltage at once, find the shared substation first; the root repair restores all dependents at once.

title: Partial restoration deprioritized the substation too early — August 2026
summary: The grid_voltage recovered to 65% and the incident was lowered in priority before the breaker bank was fully repaired. The voltage collapsed again minutes later.
outcome: A second blackout peak hit the dependents. Lesson: hold a substation incident open until grid_voltage stays stable above 90% for 5 minutes; a partial reading is not a repair.

title: Crew diverted from the substation to a hospital — October 2026
summary: The only crew repairing the origin substation was pulled to a hospital emergency, so every dependent stayed dark longer than the hospital emergency alone would have caused.
outcome: The grid_voltage stayed low for 25 more minutes. Lesson: only divert the crew away from the origin substation if the new destination's human cost outweighs the blackout it prolongs for every dependent.

title: Fuel exhaustion stranded the repair crew — December 2026
summary: The crew's vehicle ran out of fuel on the way to a substation because the assigned refuel station had no stock, and the repair did not start.
outcome: A tanker was rerouted and the crew resumed 21 minutes later. Lesson: confirm the repair crew's own fuel and its refuel station before dispatch; a crew that cannot reach the switchyard is not a repair.

title: Faulty grid_voltage reading hid the collapse — January 2026
summary: A faulty grid_voltage sensor reported 88% while the feeder was actually at 9%, so the substation was not escalated until a field report contradicted the reading.
outcome: The crew started 15 minutes late. Lesson: corroborate an isolated healthy grid_voltage reading with field reports before trusting it; one faulty sensor can hide a full collapse.

title: Preventive repair on a declining grid_voltage trend — March 2026
summary: The substation's grid_voltage declined slowly for 20 minutes but never crossed the critical threshold. A crew was sent on the trend alone and caught the fault before it cascaded.
outcome: No dependent lost power. Lesson: a sustained grid_voltage decline at a substation justifies a preventive crew; a slow feeder fault is cheaper to stop before it cascades.

title: Two substations failed and only one crew existed — May 2026
summary: Two substations in different rings failed within minutes and only one crew was available. The crew was committed to the ring with more dependents first while the other grid_voltage kept falling.
outcome: The second ring stayed dark 30 minutes longer but the wider ring recovered first. Lesson: with one crew and two failed substations, repair the one with more dependents first and hold the other with generators on its critical sites.
